analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal campaign finance rules, capping party 'soft money' donations while doubling individual contribution limits.
analysis.headline: Senator Warner's campaign finance bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in the Senate Rules Committee without a vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap the unlimited 'soft money' donations flowing to national party committees at $100,000 per person per year, ban campaign donations from foreign nationals and anyone not eligible to register to vote, and bar candidates from spending campaign funds on personal expenses like mortgages, tuition, or country club dues. It also doubles the individual contribution limit from $1,000 to $2,000 per candidate and raises limits on giving to national parties, adds a tax credit for small donations, and requires corporations to tell shareholders about political donations. Separately, it would require union members to give written consent before their dues fund politics, and would roll back parts of the 1993 voter registration law, including ending mandatory mail-in registration and letting states require photo ID.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates facing wealthy self-funded opponents get higher contribution limits to compete; taxpayers who give up to $100 to in-state congressional candidates get a tax credit; shareholders learn where corporate political money goes; voters get faster online access to campaign finance reports; party committees gain doubled hard-money limits even as soft money is capped.

how_it_helps.text: Caps 'donations' — the unlimited soft money given to national party committees — at $100,000 per person per calendar year, ending the era when a single donor could give millions outside normal limits.

Bans campaign contributions and donations from foreign nationals, from domestic subsidiaries of foreign companies that cannot show separate funding, and from any individual not eligible to register to vote in federal elections.

Prohibits converting campaign funds to personal use, expressly banning spending on home mortgages, rent, tuition, vacations, country club memberships, and other expenses that would exist regardless of the campaign.

Creates a tax credit of up to $100 per person ($200 joint) for contributions to congressional candidates in the taxpayer's own state, available only to households earning under $60,000 ($120,000 joint).
Requires corporations that file annual reports to shareholders to disclose the total amount of political donations and the committees that received them.
Requires registered lobbyists to disclose contributions and donations in their semiannual reports and directs the FEC to post campaign finance reports on the Internet.

Doubles the per-candidate contribution limit from $1,000 to $2,000 and lets candidates raise up to four times the normal limits from individual donors if an opponent spends more than $25,000 of personal money.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions lose automatic use of members' dues for political activity, since written consent would be required and members could sue for double the amount collected without it. Large donors and party committees lose uncapped soft money above $100,000. Voters lose automatic mail-in registration, must give a Social Security number and proof of citizenship to register, and could face photo ID requirements. States take on new registration and voter-list rules.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the individual contribution limit to $2,000 and raising limits on giving to national party committees from $20,000 and $25,000 to $50,000 channels more large-donor money into campaigns even as the bill caps soft money.

Repealing the federal requirement for voter registration by mail, requiring proof of citizenship and Social Security numbers, and letting states purge registrants who skip elections and demand photo ID would make registering and voting harder for many Americans.

Requiring written consent before union dues fund non-representational political activity, with double-damage lawsuits, was structured to sharply reduce labor's political spending while corporations faced only a disclosure requirement for their donations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The soft money cap, foreign-money ban, personal-use ban, and disclosure provisions are genuine anti-corruption measures that would have shed light on and limited big political money. But the same bill raises hard-money limits in ways that favor large donors, and its voting provisions would restrict registration access for ordinary citizens. The union consent requirement hit one side of politics (organized labor) with mandates while giving corporate political spending only a disclosure rule. On balance it traded a real soft-money crackdown for provisions that shifted power toward individual large donors and restricted voting access.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Warner introduced the bill on November 13, 1997, during the campaign finance debate that followed the 1996 election cycle, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
The Rules and Administration Committee took no further action, and the bill never came to the Senate floor before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large soft-money donors and national party committees kept the existing uncapped soft-money system, and unions kept using dues for politics without written consent. Anyone hoping for a compromise campaign finance law in that Congress got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big soft-money donors and party committees

for.name: Sen. John Warner
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-VA); sponsor and Chairman, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to the committee he chaired, which took no action on it.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on November 13, 1997, and never reported it out, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never showed up in the record; the bill died with its Republican sponsor alone.

industries.note: Unions would need written consent from every member before spending dues on political or charitable causes outside collective bargaining, with double-damages lawsuits for violations, sharply cutting labor's political war chest. Members who object to political spending would gain a direct right to stop it.

Soft money — unlimited donations to national parties — would be capped at $100,000 per person per year, but hard-money limits on party giving would double to $50,000. Parties would trade unlimited big checks for a higher ceiling on regulated money.
They would lose the ability to give unlimited soft money but gain doubled candidate contribution limits ($2,000) and doubled party limits, keeping more of their money inside the legal channels.

They would face a new duty to disclose aggregate political donations and recipient committees to shareholders — transparency only, no restriction — while foreign-owned subsidiaries would face clearer bans on political giving.

Senators could not use taxpayer-funded mass mailings (the franking privilege) in their own election years, and could no longer convert campaign funds to personal use like mortgages, cars, or club dues.
